catalog_quote: Stress appears to have been an important factor in the pronunciation of Yorta Yorta words. Curr (Cb:582-583), in his word list for Bangerang proper, places bars above one syllable in each word ... It appears that these bars indicate the stress in each word. ... Curr's (Cb:579) following examples illustrate that word stress can change under affixation: 'grass' bārpan /bárrpan/; 'to search for grass' barpānyanook /barbányanug/; 'a minnow' jāwa /djáwa/; 'to fish for minnows' jawānyanook /djawányanug/. It thus seems that the addition of the suffix /-nyanug/ shifts the stress from the first to the second syllable. In every case where Curr lists a two-syllable word, the stress falls on the first syllable, but where the word has more than two syllables, the pattern is less consistent. new_statements.quote: In every case where Curr lists a two-syllable word, the stress falls on the first syllable, but where the word has more than two syllables, the pattern is less consistent. Suffixes appear to cause the shift of stress to the second syllable, but there are some three-syllable words where the stress remains on the first syllable. [...] Elsewhere in this work and in the vocabulary lists we have notated syllable stress on the phonemic representation of multisyllable words where the sources provide us with information that stress is other than syllable-initial using an acute accent over the vowel of the accented syllable (e.g. /barbanyanug/ 'grass').

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default (unmarked) stress is on the first syllable of the word: every disyllable in Curr's Bangerang list is initially stressed, and the authors mark stress in the grammar and vocabulary only when it is NOT initial. In longer words the picture is less regular: several suffixes move the stress to the second syllable (verbaliser -nyanug: /barbanyánug/ 'search for grass', /djawanyánug/ 'fish for minnows'; past -banga: /malínbanga/ 'I did hit'; reciprocal past /malédhan/, where the stress shift alone marks past; diminutive -unga/-idjiga: /djondúnga/ 'little bird'; future/imperative of malin 'hit'), while some three-syllable words keep initial stress. The whole account is inferred from Curr's bars and Mathews' inverted commas in 19th-century transcriptions, so the authors hedge ('appears', 'seems').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by Bowe & Morey. Hercus 1986:162 (phonetic notes on Yodayoda) refers to vowels 'under the secondary stress' being half-long but does not say where secondary stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixed/derived words: -nyanug, past -banga, reciprocal past, diminutive formatives -unga/-idjiga, and future/imperative verb forms shift stress to the second syllable (pp. 52-53, 84, 89, 97); 'some three-syllable words' keep initial stress; the word for 'one' (y)iyawa reconstructed with second-syllable stress from the spelling iawa (p. 40).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation/wordlist forms, reconstructed philologically for an extinct language from 19th-century orthographic stress marks (Curr 1887 'Cb', Mathews notebooks/1902) plus Hercus's 1960s recordings of the last semi-speakers. The acute accents on the phonemic forms in the book (e.g. /barbanyánug/) were dropped by the PDF text layer; the quote reproduces the scanned text. Confidence is medium because the authors themselves present the pattern as an inference from source diacritics.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes Yorta Yorta (Bangerang) as a whole, drawing mainly on Curr's 'Bangerang proper' wordlist (Cb), Mathews' 'Yota Yota' (RMa/RMb) and Hercus's 1960s Yodayoda recordings; the stress statement is based chiefly on Curr's Bangerang-proper data. The book also covers the closely related Yabula Yabula (Ngarimoro) in a separate section, which is a distinct Glottolog languoid (code not checked here). Hercus 1986 'Yodayoda' = the same language.

sources.citation: Curr, Edward M. 1887. The Australian Race, vol. 3. Melbourne: Government Printer. 'Goulburn: The Bangerang tribes proper', pp. 566-583 (Curr's own wordlists; the 'Cb' source of Bowe & Morey).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Primary raw data: Curr placed bars over one syllable per word to mark stress (per Bowe & Morey p. 52); the bars do not survive scanned and the Bangerang prefatory remarks contain no prose statement about accent (the only accent remarks in the volume are in other contributors' Queensland entries).
Alternate names Yodayoda, Yota Yota, Bangerang, Echuca, Moira etc; lists Bowe & Morey 1999 (grammar) and Locke 1878 (sketch) as the descriptive sources; nothing on stress.
